title: Customers with No Orders
description:
Return customers who have **never placed an order**, using NOT EXISTS.

**Table: customers**

| Column | Type |
|--------|------|
| id | INT |
| name | VARCHAR |
| email | VARCHAR |
| city | VARCHAR |
| country | VARCHAR |

**Table: orders**

| Column | Type |
|--------|------|
| id | INT |
| customer_id | INT |
| order_date | DATE |
| status | VARCHAR |
| total_amount | DECIMAL |

Output columns: `id`, `name`. Order by `name`.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, name VARCHAR, email VARCHAR, city VARCHAR, country VARCHAR); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Alice','alice@example.com','New York','USA'),(2,'Bob','bob@example.com','London','UK'),(3,'Carol','carol@example.com','Chicago','USA'),(4,'Dan','dan@example.com','Mumbai','India'); CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, customer_id INT, order_date DATE, status VARCHAR, total_amount DECIMAL); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,DATE '2026-01-05','completed',100.00),(2,3,DATE '2026-03-15','pending',50.00);
solution_sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY name

test_cases.description: Bob and Dan have no orders

hints: NOT EXISTS is the logical inverse of EXISTS — it is TRUE when the subquery returns no rows.
This is often more readable than a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL approach.
explanation: `NOT EXISTS (...)` is TRUE when no matching orders row exists for that customer. Bob and Dan have no orders rows, so they are returned.
